conflicts.name: Close-hauled
conflicts.text: Source says about 45 degrees close-hauled; the simulation's no-go half-width is about 36 degrees (Falua sails from about 35-40, 3.6 kn at 45), and the Rabelo needs 50 degrees.

conflicts.name: Leeboard
conflicts.text: Existing concept describes a board lowered to reduce slip in shallow water. The candidate (tábua de bolina) describes a lateral keel on one side, one per side on the muleta, for lateen-rigged flat-bottomed boats; it also adds dates (documented 1710, on other boats 1785) not in the existing concept. Possibly complementary rather than conflicting.

conflicts.name: Gust
conflicts.text: Method doc defines a gust as a sudden increase in wind. Fragateiro's gust_or_shift also includes changes in wind direction.

conflicts.name: Beating to windward
conflicts.text: Source gives 45–50 degrees to the wind while beating; the simulation has a no-go half-width of about 36 degrees (Falua nothing below about 35, Rabelo 50), so the figures differ by boat.

conflicts.name: Downwind sail setting rule
conflicts.text: Source says set sails at 90 degrees to the wind downwind; the simulation states no matching sail angle, and its sheet stop is 20 degrees.

conflicts.name: Bateiras (cargo boats)
conflicts.text: c278 'Bateiras' is described as cargo boats, while the candidate (Embarcações do Rio Tejo) describes bateiras as boats of Avieiro fishing communities that they also lived aboard; c349 describes a bateira as a small boat on the Lisbon run.

conflicts.name: Batel passenger limit
conflicts.text: The source gives two different passenger limits for the batel: 8 persons (paragraph 19) and 12 persons (paragraph 61).

conflicts.name: Scheduled service boat (barco da carreira)
conflicts.text: The sources give differing counts: one boat per week on the Lisbon run, 2-4 barcas per route, and 100 Abrantes boats in 1552.

conflicts.name: Estuary navigation (tidal reach)
conflicts.text: Candidates 1 and 2 give 20-30 km upstream of Lisbon as the limit of significant traffic, while candidate 37 says boats operated longest where the tide reaches (Sabugueiro, per candidates 11 and 12), a much longer reach; the tidal extent is stated differently.

conflicts.name: Square sail no-go angle
conflicts.text: Candidate 28 says the Rabelo's square sail cannot sail closer than about 50° to the wind, while candidate 29 says a square sail can be braced to 35°. Both describe the square-rig limit, so the numbers differ.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): In the early 15th century Almada and Ribatejo (Montijo) linked Lisbon with the south, with Coina also important; fish from Setúbal and Arrábida came through them.

practices.why: No royal travel route between Almeirim and Lisbon.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Large quantities of melons from the Santarém and Abrantes lezírias were carried to Lisbon as a new item; wine arrived by river, named after loading ports.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT ([page 2]): Three barcas and batéis came from Vila Nova da Rainha to Lisbon two to three times a week.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 160): In the mid-19th century Portuguese boats, mostly from Rossio de Abrantes, Pego and Alvega, carried Alcántara ore to Lisbon in convoys of at least ten boats so crews could help each other with towing at rapids.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 161): Larger boats could not navigate in dry season, even at Abrantes; in summer timber and cork went by raft to Salvaterra de Magos or Valada, then by boat to Lisbon.

evidence: - jorgeGasparOsportosfluviaisdoT (page 183): Timber received first treatment at the felling site: felled trees were cleaned and trunks sorted by size, reducing mass and transport cost before shipping.
